summary: Ihya Ulum al-Din ('The Revival of the Religious Sciences') by Imam Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (d. 505 AH / 1111 CE) is one of the most celebrated and influential works in Islamic literature. It offers a comprehensive treatment of Islamic worship, manners, and spirituality, aiming to revive the inner dimension of religion. It is widely read across the Sunni world but has also attracted scholarly criticism on hadith grounds — readers should be aware of the views of hadith scholars regarding some of its narrations.
overview:
Ihya Ulum al-Din ('The Revival of the Religious Sciences') by Imam Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (450–505 AH / 1058–1111 CE) is among the most celebrated and widely read works in Islamic intellectual history. Al-Ghazali was a Shafi'i jurist, Ash'ari theologian, and philosopher who taught at the Nizamiyyah Academy in Baghdad — then the most prestigious Islamic institution — before undergoing a spiritual crisis that led him to withdraw from public life, travel, and compose this monumental work.

The Ihya is divided into four quarters (rub'): (1) Acts of Worship (Rubu' al-Ibadat) — covering purity, prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, and Quranic recitation from an inner-dimension perspective; (2) Social Customs (Rubu' al-Adat) — covering eating, marriage, travel, listening to music, and commanding right and forbidding wrong; (3) The Destructive Vices (Rubu' al-Muhlikat) — covering the diseases of the soul: arrogance, envy, avarice, ostentation, and love of the world; (4) The Saving Virtues (Rubu' al-Munjiyat) — covering repentance, patience, gratitude, fear, hope, love of God, and the remembrance of death.

Al-Ghazali's project was to reunite the outer (zahir) and inner (batin) dimensions of Islamic practice that he saw as having become separated in his era — jurists focused on the outward law without spiritual content, while Sufi practitioners engaged in inner work without grounding in the law. The Ihya integrates both, presenting each act of worship as simultaneously a legal obligation and a spiritual opportunity.

**Scholarly Caution:** The Ihya contains a significant number of weak (da'if) and fabricated (mawdu') hadith. Imam al-Iraqi (d. 806 AH) wrote a full-length commentary, Takhrij Ahadith al-Ihya, documenting the hadith grades throughout the book — many narrations are graded as weak or baseless. Imam al-Dhahabi and others noted this criticism. Readers should use the Ihya for its spiritual insights and ethical framework while exercising caution about treating its narrations as evidence in religious rulings without independent verification. This concern does not negate the work's spiritual and intellectual value, which has been recognised by scholars including Ibn Taymiyyah (who praised its moral sections while criticising its philosophical and Sufi-speculative elements) and contemporary scholars across the Sunni world.
